subject: English
passage: Chronic occupational stress is typically assessed through multi-week ambulatory cortisol sampling, an expensive and burdensome procedure that requires participants to collect saliva at fixed intervals throughout each workday. In a 2018 study, Chanthira Mukherjee and colleagues demonstrated that brief laboratory tasks involving simulated workplace pressures reliably elicit measurable reductions in heart-rate variability (HRV) among office employees. Building on this, Narong Santos has hypothesized that lab-induced HRV responses in such employees could serve as a valuable proxy for ambulatory cortisol measurements, sparing organizations and workers the considerable cost and disruption associated with the longitudinal sampling currently favored in occupational health research.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis presented in the text?

choices.A: Compared with cortisol-monitored employees, employees assessed via the lab HRV task can withstand significantly higher workloads before reporting any subjective distress.
choices.B: Lab-induced HRV responses tend to vary more from individual to individual than do ambulatory cortisol levels when employees are exposed to similar workplace pressures.
choices.C: Under comparable workplace conditions, lab-induced HRV responses and ambulatory cortisol levels show comparable patterns of stress-related change.
choices.D: It is easier to detect mild HRV changes in lab-task participants than it is to detect severe cortisol elevations in employees undergoing ambulatory sampling.

explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it presents a finding that, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis that lab-induced HRV responses could serve as a valuable proxy for ambulatory cortisol measurements. The text explains that organizations currently rely on costly, intrusive multi-week cortisol sampling to assess chronic occupational stress. The hypothesis proposes that brief lab HRV measurements could replace that procedure. For the lab measure to function as a reliable proxy, it would need to produce results that accurately track what the cortisol measure would show under similar conditions. A finding that, under comparable workplace conditions, HRV responses and cortisol levels show comparable patterns of stress-related change would directly support the hypothesis, since it would establish that measuring HRV in the lab would reliably indicate the cortisol patterns that ambulatory sampling would reveal.
